main_damage_causes: Transfer of Moody's most characterful lines and command functions to other characters (primarily Tonks and Sirius), hollowing out his distinctive voice and authority
Removal of the Order photograph scene — Moody's only relationship-building moment with Harry — which eliminates his emotional complexity and his role as a living link to the first war
Compression or omission of the post-death mourning arc, preventing Moody's death from registering as the saga-level loss the books intend it to be

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (Order arrival at Privet Drive / Grimmauld Place briefing) — Moody's lines reassigned to Tonks
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 36-100 establish Moody as the commanding, hypervigilant leader of the escort operation: he issues all orders, applies the Disillusionment Charm, controls the Put-Outer, directs flight paths, and speaks far more than any other member. He is unambiguously in charge.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film corpus (Scene 1), several of Moody's lines and command functions are absorbed into other characters. Tonks speaks the line 'All right, all right! You'll all have time for a cozy catch-up later!' — a line that in the book belongs to Moody. Moody's on-screen role in the arrival scene is reduced to brief interjections rather than sustained command leadership.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Moody's defining function in OotP is as the consummate tactical commander — every decision in the escort is his. Transferring his signature line and authority cues to Tonks flattens his leadership presence at one of his most characterful moments and dilutes the audience's understanding of who he is and why his death will matter.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (Deathly Hallows Part 1 kitchen briefing) — Moody's multi-scene commanding voice compressed and partially re-attributed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 263-325 show Moody dominating the Seven Potters briefing across an extended sequence: explaining the Trace, the transport plan, the Polyjuice logistics, pairing assignments, and issuing the countdown. He is repeatedly assertive, darkly humorous, and authoritative over many exchanges.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 5 (the script) shows the briefing compressed significantly. The line 'All right, all right! You'll all have time for a cozy catch-up later!' is given to Tonks in the film script rather than Moody. Moody's lines are present but condensed, and the extended multi-beat authority he displays across the book sequence is truncated.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Moody fills the briefing with paranoid, darkly comic asides ('tastes like goblin piss,' extended threats to Mundungus, careful tactical reasoning). The film compresses this to functional exposition. His voice — gruff, darkly funny, relentlessly suspicious — is thinned to plot delivery, reducing his distinctiveness.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 — Moody's paranoid tactical reasoning ('Death Eaters will expect the real Harry to be with the most skilled Auror') transferred to Lupin post-mortem
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 348 (via Tonks reporting): 'Mad-Eye said he'd expect the real Harry to be with the toughest, most skilled Aurors. He chased Mad-Eye first.' This is Moody's own pre-mission strategic deduction, demonstrating his tactical self-awareness and courage — he knowingly made himself the primary target.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 8: Lupin delivers this explanation after Moody's death — 'Mad-Eye reckoned You-Know-Who would expect the real Harry to be with the most skilled Auror. He knew he'd be in the most danger.' While the content survives, it is delivered as reported speech by Lupin, not shown as Moody's live reasoning during the briefing.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book gives audiences the chance to understand Moody's courage as a conscious, pre-meditated choice he made knowing the risk. In the film this arrives only as posthumous explanation, removing the dramatic weight of watching a man knowingly accept the most dangerous position. The courage reads as fact rather than character revelation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 (Weasley house after the flight) — Moody's death announced but his absence from the emotional aftermath is total
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 340-414 devote sustained space to collective grief, Harry's personal meditation on Moody ('so tough, so brave, the consummate survivor'), the toast, Lupin's mission to recover the body, Harry burying the magical eye, and the lingering 'shock of losing Mad-Eye' over days. Moody's death is treated as a saga-level loss.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 8 announces the death efficiently ('Mad-Eye's dead') and Scene 9 contains a single reference ('Suppose it's him that did Mad-Eye'). The film corpus contains no equivalent of the extended mourning, the toast, the eye burial, or Harry's ongoing grief and guilt.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Moody's death in the books is the saga's first Order-of-the-Phoenix casualty of the final war, used to establish genuine stakes and Harry's sense of loss and guilt. Stripping the aftermath to a brief announcement and one passing reference means the audience cannot feel the weight of the loss, undermining both Moody's importance and the emotional groundwork for the rest of Deathly Hallows.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 12/13 (Ministry infiltration) — Moody's eye on Umbridge's door present but context of Harry's reaction compressed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 404-414 show Harry's visceral, multi-beat reaction to finding Moody's eye on Umbridge's door — he forgets where he is, strides forward involuntarily, feels rage, and later makes the personal decision to retrieve and bury the eye as an act of respect. This is an intimate character moment linking Harry's grief to action.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scenes 12/13 show the eye on the door and Harry's anger (jaw tightens), and he retrieves it (implied by later reference in Scene 9's cafe sequence). The retrieval and burial are present in the book corpus's later scenes but the film corpus shows only the discovery beat; the personal grief-driven decision-making is not dramatised on screen.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the eye discovery as a moment where Harry's grief for Moody becomes active and personal — he does something for Moody that no one else did. The film reduces this to a functional story beat (retrieving a plot-relevant object), losing the emotional continuity between Moody's death and Harry's ongoing mourning.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (OotP — Grimmauld Place briefing) — Moody's Order photograph scene entirely absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 129-144 show Moody producing the original Order of the Phoenix photograph, naming every member, many of them dead or destroyed, and Harry's complex emotional reaction — seeing his parents alongside Wormtail, surrounded by the doomed. This is Moody's primary relationship-building scene with Harry and his key characterisation as a keeper of memory and history.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus (OotP, Scene 2) reassigns the photograph scene entirely to Sirius, who gives Harry the Order photo at King's Cross. Moody is not involved. The book's version — Moody producing it from his pocket during the party, naming the dead, being 'under the impression he had just given Harry a bit of a treat' — is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The photograph scene is Moody's single most important one-on-one moment with Harry in OotP. It establishes Moody as a man shaped by loss, a living link to Harry's parents' generation, and creates the closest thing to warmth between them. Transferring it to Sirius removes Moody's emotional complexity and severs the only scene where his relationship with Harry deepens beyond tactical command.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (OotP) — Moody's 'Don't put your wand there, boy / lost buttocks' exchange and wand-safety characterisation absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 46-48 show Moody's gruff, darkly comic wand-safety lecture ('Better wizards than you have lost buttocks'), his irritable awareness of Tonks rolling her eyes, and his stumping off — a brief but highly characteristic moment showing his paranoid-yet-grounded personality and his odd rapport with the group.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene appears in the film corpus for OotP. Moody's arrival at Privet Drive and conduct in the kitchen is reduced to brief lines about the rescue and the plan.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The buttocks exchange is emblematic of Moody's unique voice — the blend of genuine paranoia and dark comedy that makes him memorable. Without moments like this, film Moody reads as a generic tough-commander rather than the eccentric, irreplaceable character the books portray.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (OotP) — Moody's Disillusionment Charm, Put-Outer use, and sustained tactical flight command absent or unattributed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 62-101 show Moody casting the Disillusionment Charm on Harry, deploying the Put-Outer borrowed from Dumbledore, directing flight headings throughout the journey, and being the last one inside before closing the door. These are distinct demonstrations of Moody's competence, preparation, and singular authority.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1 (OotP) shows only the arrival at Grimmauld Place via a brief visual montage. None of the flight command, the Disillusionment Charm, or the Put-Outer appear in the film corpus. The entire flight sequence is elided.
damaging_scenes.explanation: These scenes are where the book shows rather than tells Moody's reputation as the finest Auror of his generation. Without them, his tactical brilliance and the reason everyone defers to him are asserted but never demonstrated, making his authority feel inherited by reputation rather than earned on screen.
